summary.text:
The paper set is a 6-page covering report (92921) and a 23-page Appendix C (92924) that carries the substantive detail. Both were read. The covering paper is not thin — it carries Tables 1-6 including the financing-cost ratio table. Appendix C carries the portfolio position, the MUFG adviser rate view dated 22 December 2025, the borrowing strategy, the maturity schedule, and the MRP policy including a £16.181m cumulative VRP overpayment disclosure. No per-loan schedule is published and no weighted rate for the PWLB book appears anywhere in either paper.

The loan-book reconciles cleanly on the maturity schedule. We hold eight PWLB loans totalling £55.877m; the paper's Section 3.5 table sums to £55.87m, and its 20-to-30-year bucket prints £39.20m — matching our six maturity loans running to 2052-2057 to the pound. The four short-end buckets rebuild from the ~£1.04m of annual principal amortising on the one EIP loan (£16.66m at 3.03% to 2042). We cannot cross-check the weighted rate because the paper doesn't print one.

The loan book is a three-tier barbell: the £16.66m cheap amortising EIP; two 4.60%-4.75% maturity loans totalling £23.9m to 2052; and four legacy loans at 7.00%-7.88% totalling £15.30m to 2055-2057. On the DMO's repayment curve today the net position is only £828k below par because £3.9m of premium on the four 7%+ loans offsets £4.7m of discount on the newer loans almost pound for pound. That is an unusually flat position — most books we've priced this year sit several million below par with no material premium anywhere.

The paper self-flags the Non-HRA financing cost ratio at c.25% against an LGA average of c.14%. It sits at 15.5% now, rises to 21.8% next year, and plateaus at 24.1-24.3% for three years running. The HRA ratio falls from 15.8% to 12.4% as the HRA CFR amortises down in £1.04m chunks — the same amortising EIP loan seen from the other side of the report. The borrowing stance is set against a MUFG forecast that has since gone the wrong way — long PWLB certainty is 44-53bp higher than the adviser's 22 December spot, not lower — which reinforces the §3.4 reasoning to use internal cash and short-dated LA-to-LA money until PWLB rates come down.

officer.body:
Hi Paul,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Treasury Management Strategy that went to Council on 25 February. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first, and it came out well. We hold eight PWLB loans for Lancaster totalling £55,876,946. Your Section 3.5 maturity table sums to £55.87m and its 20-to-30-year bucket prints £39.20m; we hold six maturity loans running to 2052-2057 that total £39,200,000 to the pound. The four short-end buckets (£1.04m, £1.04m, £3.12m, £5.21m) rebuild from the £1.04m of annual principal amortising on your one EIP loan through 2042. You don't print a weighted rate anywhere, so we've kept rate comparisons out.

The interesting thing in your book is the shape underneath. It sits in three tiers: an £16.66m EIP at 3.03% to 2042, two maturity loans at 4.60% and 4.75% totalling £23.9m to 2052, and four legacy loans at 7.00% to 7.88% totalling £15.30m to 2055-2057. On the DMO's premature repayment curve today the net position is £828k below par: about £4.7m of discount on the 3.03%-4.75% loans, offset almost pound for pound by £3.9m of premium on the four 7% loans. Books we've priced this year almost all sit several million below par with no material premium anywhere. Yours carries £3.9m of premium on 27% of the principal. Standard caveats: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. The pricing is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

Your borrowing stance is set against the MUFG 22 December forecast that Bank Rate would fall to 3.25% by December and the long end would follow. Eight months on, Bank Rate is still 3.75% and long PWLB certainty rates are 44 to 53 basis points higher than that spot, not lower. So the reasoning at paragraph 3.4 — internal cash and short-dated LA-to-LA money until PWLB rates reduce — has been reinforced, not weakened. Inter-authority lending is the market that sits between DMADF safety and credit risk, and it's the one nobody publishes. We track it across the sector, so what other authorities are actually paying for one-month, three-month and six-month money is visible rather than inferred. That's at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

One small note, offered because we'd want to know. Your Section 2.5 discloses £16.181m of cumulative VRP overpayments to 31 March 2025 — £13.533m HRA, £2.648m General Fund — reclaimable in later years. Most councils we have read don't disclose a running VRP balance at all. Whether anything's worth doing with it is a Council policy call; we mention it because the disclosure itself is unusually candid.

On training, four fit Lancaster. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets goes to the market paragraph 3.4 plans to use before returning to PWLB. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator goes to the pricing above. Money Market Funds (CNAV / LVNAV / VNAV) covers what 58% of your £29.3m investment book actually is. Liability benchmark deep dive works alongside Section 2.3. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 (covering report and Appendix C), Council, 25 February 2026.
